## Statistical Inference: Distributional Comparisons Across Years and Journey Types

Section 4.1 established descriptive differences in travel-mode composition across Census years and journey types. This section formalises those observations using Pearson’s chi-square tests to evaluate whether observed differences represent statistically detectable distributional divergence. Given the extremely large national Census counts, statistical significance is interpreted alongside effect size (Cramér’s V) to distinguish detectability from substantive magnitude.

### Time-Based Change Within Education (2018 vs 2023)

**Is there statistically significant evidence that the distribution of travel modes for Education changed between 2018 and 2023?**

The Pearson chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between Census year and travel category within Education journeys ($\chi^2(4) = 13{,}501, p < 0.001$). Since $p < 0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis that the distribution of Education travel modes was identical in 2018 and 2023. This indicates that education-related travel behaviour underwent statistically detectable structural redistribution over the five-year period.


```{r include=FALSE, ref.label="test_time_shift_funtion"}
```
```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="edu_chi-square_test_tbl"}
```


### Time-Based Change Within Work (2018 vs 2023)

**Is there statistically significant evidence that the distribution of travel modes for Work changed between 2018 and 2023?**

The Pearson chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between Census year and travel category within Work journeys ($\chi^2(4) = 66,534, p < 0.001$). Since $p < 0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis that the distribution of Work travel modes was identical in 2018 and 2023. This indicates that work-related travel patterns experienced substantial structural change between Census waves.


```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="work_chi-square_test_tbl"}
```


### Cross-Journey Comparison in 2018

**Is there statistically significant evidence that the distribution of travel modes differed between Education and Work in 2018?**


The Pearson chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between journey type and travel category in 2018 ($\chi^2(4) = 517,341, p < 0.001$). Since $p < 0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis that Education and Work shared the same travel-mode distribution in 2018. This confirms that baseline modal composition differed structurally between students and workers prior to the pandemic period.


```{r include=FALSE, ref.label="test_edu_vs_work_by_year_funcion"}
```

```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="chi_edu_work_2018"}
```


### Cross-Journey Comparison in 2023

**Is there statistically significant evidence that the distribution of travel modes differed between Education and Work in 2023?**

The Pearson chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between journey type and travel category in 2023 ($\chi^2(4) = 572,042, p < 0.001$). Since $p < 0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis that Education and Work shared the same travel-mode distribution in 2023. This indicates that journey-purpose differentiation in travel behaviour persisted in the post-pandemic period.


```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="chi_edu_work_2023"}
```


### Effect Size for Cross-Journey Differences

Because Census counts are extremely large, statistical significance alone does not convey substantive magnitude. Effect size is therefore assessed using Cramér’s V.

The estimated values are 0.3261 for 2018 and 0.3339 for 2023, indicating a moderate-to-strong association between journey type and travel category in both Census years. The stability of effect size across waves suggests that cross-journey structural differentiation remains substantively meaningful rather than merely statistically detectable.


```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="cramers_v_tbl"}
```



### Differential Change Between Journey Types (2018-2023)

**Is there statistically significant evidence that the change in travel-mode distributions between 2018 and 2023 differed between Education and Work journeys?**

The Pearson chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between journey type and category-wise change profiles over time ($\chi^2(4) = 91{,}461, p < 0.001$). Since p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis that Education and Work experienced identical temporal redistribution across travel categories. This indicates that the magnitude and structure of modal change between 2018 and 2023 differed systematically between journey purposes.


```{r include=FALSE, ref.label="shift_tab_function"}
```

```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="chisq_shift_tbl"}
```



**Synthesis of Inferential Findings**

Collectively, the chi-square analyses establish three consistent findings. First, both Education and Work travel-mode distributions changed significantly between 2018 and 2023. Second, Education and Work differed significantly within each Census year, with moderate-to-strong effect sizes confirming substantive journey-purpose differentiation. Third, the structure of temporal redistribution differed between journey types, indicating that post-pandemic travel adjustments were not uniform across journey purposes. Together, these results provide strong statistical evidence that travel behaviour in New Zealand underwent structurally differentiated change between 2018 and 2023.


## Multinomial Model: Differential Time-Based Change Between Education and Work

To complement the contingency-table analyses presented in Section 4.2, a multinomial logistic regression model with a $Year × Journey Type$ interaction was estimated, as described in Section 3.4.

While Section 4.2 established statistically significant distributional differences using contingency-table methods, this section provides a unified regression-based assessment of whether the 2018-2023 shifts differ systematically between Education and Work journeys.

A multinomial logistic regression model was estimated with travel category as the outcome and Census year, journey type, and their interaction as predictors. The key inferential focus is the Year × Journey Type interaction, which tests whether the temporal effect of Census year differs across journey purposes.


### Likelihood Ratio Test for Year × Journey Type Interaction

**Is there statistically significant evidence, based on the multinomial interaction model, that the change in travel-mode distributions between 2018 and 2023 differed between Education and Work journeys?**

A likelihood ratio test compared a baseline multinomial model containing only main effects (Census year and journey type) with a model including the Year × Journey Type interaction.

The likelihood ratio test showed a statistically significant improvement in model fit when the interaction term was included $(\chi^2(4) = 1320, p < 0.001)$. 

```{r include=FALSE, ref.label="model_data_function"}
```
```{r include=FALSE, ref.label="multinomial_logistic_regression_model_funtion"}
```

```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="likelihood-ratio_test"}
```




Since $p < 0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis that the time-based shift in travel-mode distribution is identical for Education and Work journeys.

This result indicates that allowing the temporal effect to differ by journey type substantially improves model fit, providing strong regression-based evidence that Education and Work underwent structurally distinct modal reallocation between 2018 and 2023.


```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="lrt_multinomial_model"}
```

### Model-Based Percentage-Point Changes in Travel Mode Shares

While the likelihood ratio test establishes statistical significance of the interaction, it does not directly convey how travel behaviour changed. To obtain interpretable effect sizes, predicted probabilities from the fitted multinomial model were computed and converted into percentage-point changes for each journey type and travel category.

The model-based predicted shares confirm distinct temporal adjustment patterns across journey types.

For Education journeys, the predicted percentage-point changes between 2018 and 2023 are as follows:


```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="pred_pp_edu_table"}
```

For Work journeys, the predicted percentage-point changes are as follows:


```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="pred_pp_work_table"}
```

These results demonstrate that although both journey types experienced increases in at-home travel, the magnitude of increase was substantially larger for Work. Conversely, Education exhibited a modest increase in private transport, whereas Work showed a pronounced decline. 

This confirms that the interaction detected by the likelihood ratio test reflects meaningful and interpretable structural divergence in modal reallocation.


### Interpretation and Synthesis

The multinomial modelling results reinforce and extend the contingency-table findings in Section 4.2. The significant interaction $(\chi^2(4) = 1320, p < 0.001)$ confirms that the 2018-2023 shift in travel-mode distribution differs between Education and Work when all travel categories are considered jointly.

Importantly, the predicted probability contrasts reveal the substantive structure of this interaction: Work journeys experienced a substantially larger shift toward at-home participation and a notable decline in private transport, whereas Education journeys underwent more moderate adjustments.

Together, the likelihood ratio test and model-based predicted probabilities provide converging evidence that post-2018 modal reallocation was not uniform across journey purposes. The regression framework therefore confirms that the observed difference-in-differences patterns reflect statistically robust and substantively meaningful divergence between Education and Work travel behaviour.




## Regional and Sub-Population Extensions

This subsection extends the national-level findings by examining whether modal redistribution between 2018 and 2023 is spatially uniform or regionally differentiated. Consistent with Section 2.5, analysis proceeds in four stages: (i) region-level distributional change, (ii) region-level percentage-point change, (iii) urban versus non-urban grouping, and (iv) regional difference-in-differences between journey purposes.

All analyses are descriptive and based on Census population counts.




### Region-Level Distributional Change

To assess whether travel-mode distributions changed within each region between the 2018 and 2023 Censuses, Pearson Chi-square tests of homogeneity were conducted separately for Journey to Education and Journey to Work.

**Table 15** below reports the region-specific Chi-square statistics, degrees of freedom, and associated p-values for both journey purposes.

```{r include=TRUE, ref.label="region-wise_pearson_chi-square_tests"}
```



Across all regions, the tests provide strong evidence of distributional change for both Education and Work. P-values are uniformly extremely small, indicating statistically detectable shifts in modal composition between Census waves. Given the population-level nature of Census data, statistical significance is expected; therefore, interpretation emphasises the relative magnitude of change rather than significance alone.

The magnitude of the Chi-square statistics varies substantially across regions. Major metropolitan regions (e.g., Auckland, Wellington, Canterbury) exhibit markedly larger statistics, particularly for Work, reflecting substantial redistribution in commuting patterns. In contrast, smaller regions display lower absolute values, although distributional change remains statistically evident.

Notably, in most regions the Chi-square statistics for Work exceed those for Education, indicating that modal restructuring between 2018 and 2023 was generally stronger for Work-related travel. This pattern is consistent with broader structural adjustments in commuting behaviour.

These results confirm that modal change occurred across all regions and for both journey purposes, motivating further examination of the magnitude and directional composition of regional percentage-point changes.


### Region-Level Percentage-Point Change

To quantify the magnitude and direction of change, percentage-point (pp) differences in mode share between 2018 and 2023 were computed for each region and journey type. Full results are reported in **Table A1 (Education) and Table A2 (Work) in the Appendix**.

Across regions, at-home participation increased for both journey types, with consistently larger gains observed for Work. The strongest increases are concentrated in major metropolitan regions, including Wellington and Auckland.

Private transport declines are more pronounced for Work than for Education in metropolitan regions, whereas Education-related private transport changes are smaller and more heterogeneous.

Public transport generally declines in high-reliance metropolitan regions, particularly for Work. Active transport also decreases in most regions, with larger reductions observed in several smaller regions for Education.

Overall, modal redistribution occurred nationwide, but the magnitude of change is greater for Work and spatially concentrated in metropolitan centres.


### Regional Difference-in-Differences

To quantify divergence between Education and Work within each region, regional difference-in-differences (DiD) measures were computed as:

$$DiD = (\Delta Education) - (\Delta Work)$$

where $\Delta$ denotes the 2018-2023 percentage-point change.

Regional DiD results are reported in **Table A7 in the Appendix**.


Positive DiD values indicate that the increase (or reduction) in mode share was larger for Education than for Work, while negative values indicate stronger change for Work.

Across regions, the largest negative DiD values occur in the **At-Home** category in major metropolitan regions, particularly Wellington and Auckland, indicating that remote participation increased substantially more for Work than for Education in these centres.

In contrast, several regions exhibit positive DiD values in **Private Transport**, reflecting stronger contraction in commuting for Work relative to Education.

Active and Public transport categories show more moderate and region-specific divergence, with both positive and negative values depending on local context.

Overall, the DiD results confirm that divergence between Education and Work is not spatially uniform and is most pronounced in metropolitan labour-market regions.


### Urban versus Non-Urban Comparisons

To assess whether settlement structure moderates modal redistribution, five major urban regions (Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Wellington, and Canterbury) and five non-urban regions (Gisborne, West Coast, Southland, Tasman, and Marlborough) were analysed separately. These classifications follow the grouping defined in Section 2.5.

#### Overall Findings for Top 5 Urban vs Non-Urban Regions

Across all analyses, three consistent conclusions emerge:

1. **Urban regions experienced substantially stronger modal redistribution**, particularly in Work travel.
2. **Remote participation expanded most sharply in metropolitan labour-market centres**, widening the Education-Work gap.
3. **Non-Urban regions exhibit greater modal stability**, with smaller difference-in-differences magnitudes and more aligned shifts across journey types.

Settlement structure therefore plays a central moderating role in post-2018 travel behaviour change, with metropolitan regions driving the majority of structural divergence between Education and Work journeys.



### City-Level Comparison

To further examine spatial heterogeneity, four representative territorial authorities were selected for focused analysis: two metropolitan centres (Wellington City and Christchurch City) and two non-metropolitan centres (Gisborne District and Invercargill City). These locations were chosen to contrast large urban labour-market hubs with smaller regional centres and to assess how travel-mode redistribution varied at a finer spatial scale beyond regional aggregation.

Percentage-point changes in travel mode shares (2018-2023) are reported in **Table A3 in the Appendix**, and the corresponding difference-in-differences (Education - Work) estimates are presented in **Table A4 (Appendix)**.

**Percentage-Point Changes**

Clear contrasts emerge across the selected cities.

In **Wellington City**, Work travel exhibits a substantial increase in *At-Home* participation (+10.56 pp), accompanied by a marked decline in *Private transport* (−5.71 pp). Education also shows increased At-Home participation (+3.79 pp) and growth in *Public transport* (+3.64 pp), while *Active transport* declines (−6.73 pp). These results indicate pronounced restructuring of commuting patterns in the capital.

In **Christchurch City**, changes are more moderate. Work At-Home participation increases by +3.92 pp, while Private transport declines by −4.00 pp. Education shows smaller shifts, including a +2.88 pp increase in At-Home participation and relatively stable modal shares elsewhere.

Among non-metropolitan centres, **Gisborne District** displays strong reductions in Education *Active transport* (−6.34 pp) and a notable increase in Education *Private transport* (+5.24 pp), suggesting modal substitution toward private vehicles. Work travel in Gisborne shows comparatively limited change.

In **Invercargill City**, modal adjustments are modest overall. Education Active transport declines (−3.89 pp), while At-Home participation increases moderately for both journey types (+2.70 pp for Education; +0.59 pp for Work). Private transport remains largely stable.

**Difference-in-Differences (Education - Work)**

Difference-in-differences estimates in **Table A4** formalise these contrasts.

Wellington City exhibits the largest divergence between journey types. The DiD for *At-Home* is −6.77 pp, indicating substantially stronger remote-work expansion relative to education. Strong positive DiD values in *Private transport* (+4.90 pp) and *Public transport* (+4.97 pp) reflect sharper contraction in commuting relative to education travel.

Christchurch City shows moderate divergence, particularly in *Private transport* (+2.94 pp), consistent with stronger commuting contraction for Work.

In Gisborne District, divergence is concentrated in *Private transport* (+4.92 pp) and *Active transport* (−5.17 pp), indicating education-specific shifts toward private modes. Invercargill City displays relatively small DiD magnitudes across categories, consistent with greater modal stability.

**Summary**

City-level evidence reinforces earlier regional findings:

* Metropolitan centres, particularly Wellington City, experienced the most pronounced divergence between Education and Work travel.
* Remote participation expanded far more strongly for Work than Education in large urban labour markets.
* Smaller regional centres exhibit more moderate and heterogeneous modal adjustments.

These results confirm that behavioural change is not only regionally differentiated but also strongly conditioned by local urban structure at the district/city level.



### Change by Age Group (Education vs Work)

This subsection examines age-specific differences in modal restructuring between 2018 and 2023. We first describe mode shares, followed by net percentage-point changes, and finally Education-Work divergence (difference-in-differences).

The Under-15 age group is included for Education journeys but is structurally excluded from Work journey comparisons, as work-related travel is not defined for this cohort in the Census data. Consequently, difference-in-differences estimates are reported only for the 15-29, 30-64, and Over 64 age groups.

For **Work**, Private transport remains dominant in both years. However, At-Home participation rises noticeably by 2023, especially among 30-64 and Over-64 workers.

#### Change in the Education-Work Gap

Education-Work divergence by age group is illustrated in **Figure BB**, with numerical values reported in **Table A6 in the Appendix**.

# Discussion

The objective of this study was to assess whether travel-mode distributions in New Zealand changed between Census 2018 and Census 2023, and whether those temporal shifts differed systematically between Education and Work journeys. Using a structured framework combining mode-share analysis, percentage-point change measurement, difference-in-differences comparison, distributional testing, and multinomial logistic modelling, the findings demonstrate clear evidence of structural modal redistribution over the post-pandemic period, with important variation across geography and age groups.

At the national level, both Education and Work journeys exhibit statistically significant changes in travel-mode composition between 2018 and 2023. However, the magnitude and pattern of these shifts differ across journey types. The most pronounced structural change occurs in the growth of *At Home* participation, particularly for Work journeys. The multinomial interaction model confirms that the temporal effect of Census year differs significantly between Education and Work journeys, providing formal statistical support for differential post-pandemic adjustment.

While both journey types experienced an expansion in remote participation, the increase is substantially larger for Work. This divergence suggests that structural remote working arrangements have persisted beyond the immediate pandemic period, whereas Education travel exhibits a comparatively smaller shift toward remote participation. The interaction effects estimated within the multinomial framework reinforce the conclusion that temporal change is not uniform across journey contexts.

The regional and sub-population extensions further clarify how national-level restructuring is spatially and demographically distributed. Metropolitan regions exhibit larger increases in *At Home* participation and sharper contractions in Private transport use relative to non-urban regions. This pattern is particularly pronounced for Work journeys, indicating that remote working capacity and modal substitution are more feasible in large urban labour markets. In contrast, non-urban regions display greater modal stability and continued reliance on Private transport, reflecting structural constraints in transport infrastructure and occupational composition.

City-level comparisons reinforce this spatial heterogeneity. Larger metropolitan centres demonstrate stronger modal redistribution, while smaller regional centres show comparatively muted change. These findings indicate that aggregate national trends are not geographically uniform but instead reflect concentrated behavioural shifts within specific spatial contexts.

Age-group analysis reveals that modal restructuring is also strongly life-stage dependent. The largest changes occur among the 30-64 and Over-64 cohorts, where *At Home* participation increases sharply and Private transport declines substantially. Younger cohorts display more moderate and parallel changes between Education and Work journeys. The widening Education-Work divergence among older adults suggests that remote working arrangements are disproportionately concentrated among prime-age and older workers, whereas education-related travel among younger populations remains more dependent on physical attendance.

Taken together, the results suggest that the post-2018 evolution of travel behaviour in New Zealand reflects a structural reconfiguration of commuting patterns rather than a temporary disruption. The persistence of remote work, particularly in metropolitan regions and among working-age adults, implies enduring implications for peak-hour congestion, transport investment planning, and public transport demand modelling.

The integration of multinomial modelling with descriptive extensions strengthens the interpretation of these findings. The regression framework provides a unified inferential test of interaction effects, while predicted probabilities translate statistical results into interpretable modal share differences. The complementary stratified analyses demonstrate how aggregate change emerges from heterogeneous demographic and spatial processes.


## Limitations

Several limitations should be acknowledged when interpreting these findings.

First, the analysis relies on aggregated Census tabulations rather than individual-level microdata. While the multinomial count formulation is statistically appropriate for grouped outcomes, it precludes adjustment for additional covariates such as income, occupation, household structure, or car ownership. As a result, the observed shifts represent distributional change across populations rather than causal behavioural responses at the individual level.

Second, Census data capture the *main* means of travel on Census day rather than habitual multi-modal behaviour. Hybrid commuting patterns or occasional travel modes may therefore be underrepresented. In particular, the rapid adoption of hybrid work arrangements may not be fully reflected in a single-day snapshot.

Third, the urban versus non-urban grouping is necessarily a simplification. Although designed to contrast metropolitan and non-metropolitan contexts, regional classification cannot fully capture within-region heterogeneity or finer-grained local transport dynamics.

Fourth, A further limitation arises from the structure of the publicly available Census tabulations. The dataset does not provide linked information on residential location and specific workplace or educational institution addresses, nor does it include trip distance or travel time. As a result, the analysis cannot assess how spatial separation between origin and destination influences modal choice or remote participation.

Fifth, attempts were made to incorporate additional contextual datasets, including the Equity Index, Deprivation Index, and urban–rural classification layers. However, mismatched spatial resolutions (e.g., meshblock versus SA2), lack of one-to-one correspondence, and missing data limited their suitability for integration within the project scope. The inability to incorporate these contextual variables restricts assessment of socioeconomic and fine-grained spatial drivers of modal change.

Sixth, the analysis spans only two Census waves. Although the 2018-2023 comparison is uniquely informative due to the pandemic context, longer-term trend analysis would require additional temporal observations to distinguish cyclical variation from structural transition.

Finally, the study focuses exclusively on Education and Work journeys. Other travel purposes, such as shopping or recreational travel, may exhibit different patterns of modal adjustment and are not examined here.

Despite these limitations, the combination of large-scale national Census data, formal interaction modelling, and systematic stratified extensions provides a robust descriptive and inferential account of post-pandemic modal restructuring in New Zealand.


## Conclusion and Future Work

This study provides comprehensive evidence that travel-mode distributions in New Zealand changed significantly between 2018 and 2023 and that these changes differ systematically between Education and Work journeys. The staged analytical design, progressing from share-based composition analysis to contingency-table testing and finally to multinomial interaction modelling, ensures that both descriptive magnitude and formal statistical interaction are evaluated. Collectively, the inferential framework establishes not only that modal distributions evolved over time, but that the magnitude and direction of change differ structurally between Education and Work journeys. The multinomial interaction model confirms that temporal shifts are not homogeneous across journey types. In particular, Work journeys exhibit substantially stronger growth in *At Home* participation relative to Education journeys.

Regional and demographic extensions reveal that these changes are unevenly distributed. Metropolitan regions and working-age adults account for a disproportionate share of modal restructuring, while non-urban regions and younger cohorts display comparatively greater stability. The Education-Work gap widens most strongly in urban labour markets and among older age groups, indicating that remote work adoption is more strongly concentrated within specific spatial and life-stage segments of the population.

These findings carry important implications for transport policy and planning. Persistent reductions in physical commuting may alter long-term demand forecasts for public transport and road infrastructure. At the same time, education-related travel remains comparatively more anchored to physical attendance, suggesting that transport strategies must differentiate between journey purposes rather than treating them as behaviourally equivalent.

Future research could extend this analysis in several directions. First, incorporating additional Census waves would allow assessment of whether observed changes represent permanent structural shifts or medium-term adjustment. Second, microdata-based modelling could examine how occupation, income, household structure, and vehicle access mediate modal transition. Third, spatial econometric approaches could explore finer-grained geographic variation below the regional level. Finally, behavioural choice models could be developed to test substitution patterns among travel modes more explicitly.

In summary, the post-pandemic period has reshaped the relationship between work, education, and mobility in New Zealand. The persistence and uneven distribution of modal change underscore the importance of journey-specific and context-sensitive transport policy in an evolving mobility landscape.

# Appendix A - R Code

```{r edu-merge-sub-files-pipeline, include=FALSE}
merge_edu_data_files <- function(files_dir, output_file) {

  files <- list.files(files_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

  final_data <- tibble()

  for (file in files) {

    file_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
    parts <- strsplit(file_name, "_")[[1]]

    region   <- parts[1]
    district <- parts[2]

    raw_data <- read.csv(file)

    delete_columns <- c(
      "STRUCTURE", "STRUCTURE_ID", "STRUCTURE_NAME", "ACTION",
      "CEN23_YEAR_001", "Observation.Value", "OBS_STATUS", "Observation.Status"
    )

    clean_data <- raw_data %>%
      select(-any_of(delete_columns)) %>%
      mutate(
        Region   = region,
        District = district,
        OBS_VALUE = coalesce(OBS_VALUE, 0)  # replace NA with 0
      )

    # 1) Summarise gender totals per group (handles missing genders & duplicates)
    gender_sums <- clean_data %>%
      group_by(Census.year, CEN23_GEO_002, CEN23_TED_002, CEN23_AGE_003) %>%
      summarise(
        male   = sum(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 1],  na.rm = TRUE),
        female = sum(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 2],  na.rm = TRUE),
        total  = sum(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 99], na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    # 2) Join back and compute "Another" (gender 3), then remove total row (99)
    clean_data_filled <- clean_data %>%
      left_join(
        gender_sums,
        by = c("Census.year", "CEN23_GEO_002", "CEN23_TED_002", "CEN23_AGE_003")
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        OBS_VALUE = if_else(
          CEN23_GEN_002 == 3,
          pmax(total - male - female, 0),
          OBS_VALUE
        )
      ) %>%
      select(-male, -female, -total) %>%
      filter(CEN23_GEN_002 != 99)

    # append the corrected data (NOT the original clean_data)
    final_data <- bind_rows(final_data, clean_data_filled)
  }

  final_data_sorted <- final_data %>%
    arrange(
      Census.year,
      CEN23_GEO_002,
      CEN23_TED_002,
      CEN23_AGE_003,
      CEN23_GEN_002
    )

  write.csv(final_data_sorted, output_file, row.names = FALSE)

  invisible(final_data_sorted)
}

```{r work-merge-sub-files-pipeline, include=FALSE}
merge_work_data_files <- function(files_dir, output_file) {

  files <- list.files(files_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
  final_data <- tibble()

  for (file in files) {

    file_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
    parts <- strsplit(file_name, "_")[[1]]

    region   <- parts[1]
    district <- parts[2]

    raw_data <- read.csv(file)

    delete_columns <- c(
      "STRUCTURE", "STRUCTURE_ID", "STRUCTURE_NAME", "ACTION",
      "CEN23_YEAR_001", "CEN23_TOI_003", "Total.personal.income",
      "Observation.Value", "OBS_STATUS"
    )

    clean_data <- raw_data %>%
      select(-any_of(delete_columns)) %>%
      mutate(
        Region   = region,
        District = district
      )

    gender_info <- clean_data %>%
      group_by(Census.year, CEN23_GEO_002, CEN23_TWO_002, CEN23_AGE_008) %>%
      summarise(
        male_calc    = sum(coalesce(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 1],  0)),
        female_calc  = sum(coalesce(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 2],  0)),
        another_calc = sum(coalesce(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 3],  0)),
        total_calc   = sum(coalesce(OBS_VALUE[CEN23_GEN_002 == 99], 0)),

        male_conf_na = any(CEN23_GEN_002 == 1 & is.na(OBS_VALUE)
                           & Observation.Status == "Confidential"),
        female_conf_na = any(CEN23_GEN_002 == 2 & is.na(OBS_VALUE)
                             & Observation.Status == "Confidential"),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    clean_data_filled <- clean_data %>%
      left_join(
        gender_info,
        by = c("Census.year", "CEN23_GEO_002", "CEN23_TWO_002", "CEN23_AGE_008")
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        OBS_VALUE = case_when(
          CEN23_GEN_002 == 1 &
            is.na(OBS_VALUE) &
            Observation.Status == "Confidential" &
            male_conf_na ~ pmax(total_calc - female_calc - another_calc, 0),

          CEN23_GEN_002 == 2 &
            !male_conf_na &
            is.na(OBS_VALUE) &
            Observation.Status == "Confidential" &
            female_conf_na ~ pmax(total_calc - male_calc - another_calc, 0),

          CEN23_GEN_002 == 3 &
            !male_conf_na & !female_conf_na &
            is.na(OBS_VALUE) ~ pmax(total_calc - male_calc - female_calc, 0),

          TRUE ~ OBS_VALUE
        )
      ) %>%
      select(
        -male_calc, -female_calc, -another_calc,
        -total_calc, -male_conf_na, -female_conf_na
      )

    final_data <- bind_rows(final_data, clean_data_filled)
  }

  # FINAL CLEANUP STEP (as requested)
  final_data_sorted <- final_data %>%
    filter(CEN23_GEN_002 != 99) %>%
    select(-Observation.Status) %>%
    arrange(
      Census.year,
      CEN23_GEO_002,
      CEN23_TWO_002,
      CEN23_AGE_008,
      CEN23_GEN_002
    )

  write.csv(final_data_sorted, output_file, row.names = FALSE)

  invisible(final_data_sorted)
}

```{r edu-transform-pipeline, include=FALSE}
### transform the travel to education dataset

transform_edu_data <- function(edu_data){
  ## 1. Rename columns
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    rename(census_year = Census.year,
           sa2_code = CEN23_GEO_002,
           sa2 = Area,
           mode_code = CEN23_TED_002,
           mode = Main.means.of.travel.to.education,
           age_group_code = CEN23_AGE_003,
           age_group = Age,
           gender_code = CEN23_GEN_002,
           gender = Gender,
           count = OBS_VALUE,
           region = Region,
           district = District
           )
  
  
  ## 2. Add travel_category column, by categorising the travel modes into 5 types
  
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    mutate(
      travel_category = case_when(
        mode %in% c(
          "Passenger in a car, truck or van",
          "Drive a car, truck or van"
        ) ~ "Private Transport",
  
        mode %in% c(
          "Bicycle",
          "Walk or jog"
        ) ~ "Active Transport",
  
        mode %in% c(
          "Public bus",
          "Train",
          "Ferry",
          "School bus"
        ) ~ "Public Transport",
  
        mode == "Study at home" ~ "At Home",
  
        mode == "Other" ~ "Other Transport",
  
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    )
  
  
  ## 3. remove the Total - gender values as these are not needed
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    filter(gender != "Total - gender")
  
  
  ## 4. replace the male female and other values in gender column
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    mutate(
      gender = recode(gender,
                      "Male / Tāne" = "Male",
                      "Female / Wahine" = "Female",
                      "Another gender / He ira kē anō" = "Other")
    )
  
  
  ## 5. Add journey_type column to indicate it is Journey to Education releated data
  edu_data$journey_type <- "Education"
  
  ## 6. Reorder the columns
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    select(
      journey_type,
      census_year,
      region,
      district,
      sa2_code,
      sa2,
      mode_code,
      mode,
      travel_category,
      age_group_code,
      age_group,
      gender_code,
      gender,     
      count
    )
  
  
  ## 7. Replace NA in student_count to 0
  
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    mutate(
      count = coalesce(count, 0)
    )
  
  
  # 8. Rename the age groups from '65 years and over' to 'Over 64 years'
  
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    mutate(
      age_group = recode(age_group,
                      "65 years and over" = "Over 64 years")
    )
  
  # 9. UTF-8 encoding on region values
  edu_data <- edu_data %>%
    mutate(
      region = recode(region,
                      "Manawatū-Whanganui Region" = "Manawatu-Whanganui Regions",
  		     "Manawatū–Whanganui Region"  = "Manawatu-Whanganui Regions")
    )
  
  write.csv(edu_data, "../../data/transformed/edu_data_transformed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  
  edu_data
}

```{r work-transform-pipeline, include=FALSE}
# transform the travel to work dataset
transform_work_data <- function(work_data){
  # 1. Rename columns
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    rename(census_year = Census.year,
           sa2_code = CEN23_GEO_002,
           sa2 = Area,
           mode_code = CEN23_TWO_002,
           mode = Main.means.of.travel.to.work,
           age_group_code = CEN23_AGE_008,
           age_group = Age,
           gender_code = CEN23_GEN_002,
           gender = Gender,
           count = OBS_VALUE,
           region = Region,
           district = District
           )
  
  # 2. Add work travel_category column, by categorising the travel modes into 5 types
  
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    mutate(
      travel_category = case_when(
        mode == "Work at home" ~ "At Home",
  
        mode %in% c(
          "Drive a private car, truck or van",
          "Drive a company car, truck or van",
          "Passenger in a car, truck, van or company bus"
        ) ~ "Private Transport",
  
        mode %in% c(
          "Public bus",
          "Train",
          "Ferry"
        ) ~ "Public Transport",
  
        mode %in% c(
          "Bicycle",
          "Walk or jog"
        ) ~ "Active Transport",
  
        mode %in% c(
          "Did not go to work today",
          "Other"
        ) ~ "Other Transport",
  
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      )
    )
  
  # 3. remove the Total - gender values as these are not needed
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    filter(gender != "Total - gender")

  
  # 4. replace the male femake and other values in gender column
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    mutate(
      gender = recode(gender,
                      "Male / Tāne" = "Male",
                      "Female / Wahine" = "Female",
                      "Another gender / He ira kē anō" = "Other")
    )

  # 5. Add journey_type column to indicate it is Journey to Education rleated data
  work_data$journey_type <- "Work"

  
  # 6. Reoder the columns
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    select(
      journey_type,
      census_year,
      region,
      district,
      sa2_code,
      sa2,
      mode_code,
      mode,
      travel_category,
      age_group_code,
      age_group,
      gender_code,
      gender,     
      count
    )
  

  # 7. Replace NA in employee_count to 0
  
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    mutate(
      count = coalesce(count, 0)
    )
  

  # 8. Rename the age groups from '65 years and over' to 'Over 64 years'
  
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    mutate(
      age_group = recode(age_group,
                      "65 years and over" = "Over 64 years")
    )

  # 9. UTF-8 encoding on region values
  unique(work_data$region)
  work_data <- work_data %>%
    mutate(
      region = recode(region,
                      "Manawatū-Whanganui Region" = "Manawatu-Whanganui Regions",
  		     "Manawatū–Whanganui Region" = "Manawatu-Whanganui Regions")
    )
  
  write.csv(work_data, "../../data/transformed/work_data_transformed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  
  work_data
}

```{r test_time_shift_funtion, include=FALSE}

test_time_shift <- function(df_one_journey) {

  tab <- df_one_journey %>%
    filter(census_year %in% c(2018, 2023)) %>%
    group_by(census_year, travel_category) %>%
    summarise(n = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = travel_category, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
    arrange(census_year)

  mat <- as.matrix(tab %>% select(-census_year))
  rownames(mat) <- tab$census_year

  out <- chisq.test(mat, correct = FALSE)

  list(table = mat, test = out)
}

res_edu_time  <- edu_work_data %>% filter(journey_type == "Education") %>% test_time_shift()
res_work_time <- edu_work_data %>% filter(journey_type == "Work") %>% test_time_shift()

# tested contingency tables
res_edu_time$table
res_work_time$table

```{r test_edu_vs_work_by_year_funcion, include=FALSE}
test_edu_vs_work_by_year <- function(data, year_value) {

  tab <- data %>%
    filter(census_year == year_value) %>%
    group_by(journey_type, travel_category) %>%
    summarise(n = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from  = travel_category,
      values_from = n,
      values_fill = 0
    ) %>%
    arrange(journey_type)

  mat <- as.matrix(tab %>% select(-journey_type))
  rownames(mat) <- tab$journey_type

  list(
    table = mat,
    test  = chisq.test(mat)
  )
}

```

```{r multinomial_logistic_regression_model_funtion, include=FALSE}
baseline_mode <- "Private Transport"

model_data <- edu_work_data %>%
  filter(census_year %in% c(2018, 2023),
         journey_type %in% c("Education", "Work")) %>%
  mutate(
    census_year = factor(census_year),
    journey_type = factor(journey_type),
    travel_category = factor(travel_category)
  )

# Set baseline for travel_category (reference outcome)
if (baseline_mode %in% levels(model_data$travel_category)) {
  model_data$travel_category <- relevel(model_data$travel_category, ref = baseline_mode)
} else {
  warning("Baseline travel_category not found. Check the exact level names in travel_category.")
  print(levels(model_data$travel_category))
}

model_data$census_year  <- relevel(model_data$census_year, ref = "2018")
model_data$journey_type <- relevel(model_data$journey_type, ref = "Work")


m0 <- nnet::multinom(travel_category ~ census_year + journey_type,
                     weights = count, data = model_data, trace = FALSE)

m1 <- nnet::multinom(travel_category ~ census_year * journey_type,
                     weights = count, data = model_data, trace = FALSE)

lrt <- anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")

```

lr_stat <- 2 * (logLik(m1) - logLik(m0))
df_diff <- attr(logLik(m1), "df") - attr(logLik(m0), "df")
p_val   <- pchisq(lr_stat, df = df_diff, lower.tail = FALSE)

lr_tbl <- tibble(
  `Likelihood Ratio Statistic` = round(as.numeric(lr_stat), 0),
  df                            = df_diff,
  p_value                       = format.pval(p_val, digits = 3, eps = 1e-16)
)

lr_tbl %>%
  kable(
    format   = "latex",

    escape   = TRUE

```{r include=FALSE}

# Define the category set
cat_levels <- c("Private Transport", "Public Transport",
                "Active Transport", "At Home", "Other Transport")

# Build prediction grid
pred_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  census_year  = factor(c(2018, 2023), levels = levels(model_data$census_year)),
  journey_type = factor(c("Education", "Work"), levels = levels(model_data$journey_type))
)

# Predict probabilities
pred_probs_wide <- predict(m1, newdata = pred_grid, type = "probs") %>%
  as_tibble()

missing_cats <- setdiff(cat_levels, names(pred_probs_wide))
if (length(missing_cats) > 0) {
  stop("These categories are missing from predicted probabilities: ",
       paste(missing_cats, collapse = ", "),
       "\nCheck levels(model_data$travel_category).")
}

pred_probs <- pred_probs_wide %>%
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(cat_levels)) %>%
  dplyr::bind_cols(pred_grid) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols      = dplyr::all_of(cat_levels),
    names_to  = "travel_category",
    values_to = "prob"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(prob_pct = round(100 * prob, 2))

# Percentage-point change from 2018 to 2023 
pred_pp <- pred_probs %>%
  dplyr::select(journey_type, census_year, travel_category, prob_pct) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from  = census_year,
    values_from = prob_pct,
    names_prefix = "y"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(pp_change_2018_2023 = y2023 - y2018) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(
  factor(journey_type, levels = c("Education", "Work")),
  travel_category
)

pander(
  pred_pp,
  caption = "Model-based predicted travel mode shares (%) in 2018 and 2023,
  and percentage-point change (2023 - 2018), by journey type and travel category"
)

```

```{r region-wise_pearson_chi-square_tests, include=FALSE}
# Helper function: run region-wise chi-square tests for a given journey type
region_chisq_by_journey <- function(data, journey_label) {

  data %>%
    filter(journey_type == journey_label, census_year %in% c(2018, 2023)) %>%
    group_by(region) %>%
    group_map(~{
      tab <- .x %>%
        group_by(census_year, travel_category) %>%
        summarise(n = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
        pivot_wider(names_from = travel_category, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
        arrange(census_year)

      mat <- as.matrix(tab %>% select(-census_year))
      rownames(mat) <- tab$census_year

      tst <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(mat))

      tibble(
        region    = .y$region,
        statistic = unname(tst$statistic),
        df        = unname(tst$parameter),
        p_value   = unname(tst$p.value)
      )
    }) %>%
    bind_rows()
}

# Education tests
region_tests_edu <- region_chisq_by_journey(edu_work_data, "Education") %>%
  rename(
    edu_statistic = statistic,
    edu_df        = df,
    edu_p_value   = p_value
  )

# Work tests
region_tests_work <- region_chisq_by_journey(edu_work_data, "Work") %>%
  rename(
    work_statistic = statistic,
    work_df        = df,
    work_p_value   = p_value
  )

# Combine into one table
region_tests_edu_work <- region_tests_edu %>%
  full_join(region_tests_work, by = "region") %>%
  arrange(pmin(edu_p_value, work_p_value, na.rm = TRUE))

# Print
region_tests_edu_work %>%
  mutate(
    edu_statistic  = formatC(edu_statistic,  format = "f", digits = 2),
    edu_p_value    = formatC(edu_p_value,    format = "e", digits = 2),
    work_statistic = formatC(work_statistic, format = "f", digits = 2),
    work_p_value   = formatC(work_p_value,   format = "e", digits = 2)
  ) %>%
  select(region,
         edu_statistic, edu_df, edu_p_value,
         work_statistic, work_df, work_p_value) %>%
  rename(
    Region                = region,
    `Edu chi_sq`    = edu_statistic,
    `Edu df`        = edu_df,
    `Edu p-value`   = edu_p_value,
    `Work chi_sq`         = work_statistic,
    `Work df`             = work_df,
    `Work p-value`        = work_p_value
  ) %>%
  kable(
    format    = "latex",
    booktabs  = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    caption   = "Region-wise Pearson chi-square tests of homogeneity for changes in travel mode distributions between 2018 and 2023"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("repeat_header", "hold_position"),
    font_size = 9
  )
```


```{r regional_mode_shares_edu_work, include=TRUE}

region_mode_share_pp <- edu_work_data %>%
  filter(census_year %in% c(2018, 2023)) %>%
  group_by(region, journey_type, census_year, travel_category) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(region, journey_type, census_year) %>%
  mutate(
    total_year = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE),
    share_pct  = 100 * n / total_year
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(region, journey_type, census_year, travel_category, share_pct) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from   = census_year,
    values_from  = share_pct,
    names_prefix = "y"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pp_change_2018_2023 = y2023 - y2018
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(c(y2018, y2023, pp_change_2018_2023), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
  arrange(journey_type, region, travel_category) %>%
  rename(
    Region                 = region,
    `Journey Type`         = journey_type,
    `Travel Category`      = travel_category,
    `2018 (%)`  = y2018,
    `2023 (%)`  = y2023,
    `PP change (2023−2018)`= pp_change_2018_2023
  )

urban_regions <- c(
  "Auckland Region",
  "Waikato Region",
  "Bay of Plenty Region",
  "Wellington Region",
  "Canterbury Region"
)

nonurban_regions <- c(
  "Gisborne Region",
  "West Coast Region",
  "Southland Region",
  "Tasman Region",
  "Marlborough Region"
)

edu_work_data_top5 <- edu_work_data %>%
  mutate(
    urban_group = case_when(
      region %in% urban_regions    ~ "Urban (Top 5)",
      region %in% nonurban_regions ~ "Non-Urban (Top 5)",
      TRUE                         ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    urban_group = factor(
      urban_group,
      levels = c("Urban (Top 5)", "Non-Urban (Top 5)", "Other")
    )
  )

    `Travel Category` = travel_category,
    `Education Δpp` = Education,
    `Work Δpp` = Work,
    `Diff-in-Diff (Education − Work, pp)` = diff_in_diff_pp
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    format    = "latex",
    booktabs  = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    caption   = "Difference-in-differences in percentage-point changes (2018–2023) between Education and Work travel mode shares for Top 5 Urban and Non-Urban regions",
    escape    = FALSE
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("repeat_header", "hold_position"),
    font_size = 9
  )

```{r include=FALSE}
chi_by_region_journey <- edu_work_data_top5 %>%
  filter(
    urban_group %in% c("Urban (Top 5)", "Non-Urban (Top 5)"),
    census_year %in% c(2018, 2023)
  ) %>%
  group_by(urban_group, region, journey_type) %>%
  group_modify(~{
    tab <- .x %>%
      group_by(census_year, travel_category) %>%
      summarise(n = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from  = travel_category,
        values_from = n,
        values_fill = 0
      ) %>%
      arrange(census_year)

    mat <- as.matrix(tab %>% select(-census_year))
    rownames(mat) <- tab$census_year

    tst <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(mat))

    tibble(
      chi_sq  = unname(tst$statistic),
      df      = unname(tst$parameter),
      p_value = tst$p.value
    )
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(urban_group, region, journey_type)

chi_by_region_journey %>%
  dplyr::mutate(p_value = formatC(p_value, format = "e", digits = 3))

```{r pp-change-by-age_group-journey, include=FALSE}
pp_change_by_group_journey <- function(data, group_vars) {

  data %>%
    filter(census_year %in% c(2018, 2023)) %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(c("journey_type", group_vars, "census_year", "travel_category")))) %>%
    summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(c("journey_type", group_vars, "census_year")))) %>%
    mutate(share = count / sum(count)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(share_pct = 100 * share) %>%
    select(journey_type, all_of(group_vars), census_year, travel_category, share_pct) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = census_year,
      values_from = share_pct,
      names_prefix = "y"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      pp_change_2018_2023 = y2023 - y2018,
      across(c(y2018, y2023, pp_change_2018_2023), ~ round(.x, 2))
    )
}

```{r include=FALSE}
delta_contrib_by_group_journey <- function(data, group_var) {

  data %>%
    filter(census_year %in% c(2018, 2023)) %>%
    group_by(journey_type, !!sym(group_var), census_year, travel_category) %>%
    summarise(n = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = census_year, values_from = n, names_prefix = "y", values_fill = 0) %>%
    mutate(delta = y2023 - y2018) %>%
    group_by(journey_type, travel_category) %>%
    mutate(
      total_delta = sum(delta, na.rm = TRUE),
      contrib_pct = ifelse(total_delta == 0, NA_real_, 100 * delta / total_delta),
      contrib_pct = round(contrib_pct, 1)
    ) %>%
    ungroup()
}
```
